name: USS Constitution
blurb: Commissioned in 1797 · nicknamed 'Old Ironsides' after War of 1812 sailors swore they saw British cannonballs bounce off her oak hull — she's still a commissioned US Navy ship today, the oldest afloat in the world.
attribution: U.S. Navy photo by Seaman Matthew R. Fairchild
source: Wikimedia Commons: USS Constitution fires a 17-gun salute.jpg
image_author: U.S. Navy photo by Seaman Matthew R. Fairchild/Released (140704-N-OG138-866)

name: United States Capitol
blurb: Its cast-iron dome was finished in 1866, after Lincoln insisted construction continue all through the Civil War as proof the Union would endure — the bronze Statue of Freedom was hoisted onto the very top in December 1863.
attribution: Architect of the Capitol; derivative work: O.J.
source: Wikimedia Commons: United States Capitol west front edit2.jpg
image_author: Architect of the Capitol; derivative work: O.J.

name: British Museum
blurb: Britain's first national public museum, opened its doors in 1759 · it has never charged general admission in over 260 years, a condition written into the founding Act of Parliament.
source: Wikimedia Commons: British Museum from NE 2 (cropped).JPG

name: Koh-i-Noor
blurb: Seized by the British East India Company in 1849 · a legend claims the diamond curses any man who wears it — every royal owner since has been a queen or queen consort.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Koh-i-noor (after 1852).png

name: Temple of Artemis
blurb: One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, rebuilt after a fire in 356 BC · legend says it burned down the same night Alexander the Great was born, allegedly torched by a man seeking eternal fame.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ephesos.jpg

name: Enola Gay
blurb: Dropped the atomic bomb 'Little Boy' on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 · pilot Paul Tibbets named the B-29 after his own mother the night before the mission.
source: Wikimedia Commons: B-29 Enola Gay w Crews.jpg

name: Lighthouse of Alexandria
blurb: Built c. 280 BC on the island of Pharos · it stood for over 1,600 years until earthquakes toppled it for good in the 14th century — no photograph or accurate scale drawing survives, only ancient descriptions and coins.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Lighthouse - Thiersch.png

name: Church of the Holy Sepulchre
blurb: This Crusader-era church was consecrated in 1149 on the site venerated as Christ's crucifixion and burial place · a wooden ladder left on a windowsill has stayed there since at least 1728, because moving it would break the fragile 'status quo' agreement between its rival Christian custodians.
source: Wikimedia Commons: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre-Jerusalem.JPG

name: Red Fort
blurb: Shah Jahan's citadel for his new capital was completed in 1648 · every Indian Prime Minister has delivered the nation's Independence Day speech from its ramparts since 1947.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Red Fort, Delhi by alexfurr.jpg

name: St Paul's Cathedral
blurb: Christopher Wren's masterpiece was completed in 1710, after the Great Fire destroyed its medieval predecessor · a 1940 photograph of its dome rising through Blitz smoke, captioned 'St Paul's Survives', became one of the most famous images of the Second World War.
source: Wikimedia Commons: St Pauls aerial (cropped).jpg

name: Chrysler Building
blurb: Completed in 1930 · its stainless-steel spire was secretly built in pieces inside the fire shaft and hoisted into place in about 90 minutes, a surprise move that let it beat a rival tower to become the world's tallest building — for less than a year.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Chrysler Building by David Shankbone Retouched.jpg

name: Colossus of Rhodes
blurb: Erected around 280 BC to celebrate Rhodes surviving a year-long siege · it toppled in an earthquake after just 54 years standing — contrary to popular legend, it never straddled the harbour entrance with ships passing beneath its legs.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Colosse de Rhodes (Barclay).jpg

name: Metropolitan Museum of Art
blurb: Founded in 1870 by a group of American businessmen, financiers and artists who wanted a national art institution to rival Europe's · its collection now spans over 5,000 years of world culture and some 2 million objects.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Metropolitan Museum of Art (The Met) - Central Park, NYC.jpg

name: Hoover Dam
blurb: Completed in 1936, two years ahead of schedule · engineers embedded cooling pipes in the concrete because a mass that size would otherwise still be curing today — it would have taken over a century to cool naturally on its own.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Ansel Adams - National Archives 79-AAB-01.jpg

name: Voynich Manuscript
blurb: Carbon-dated to 1404-1438 · its unknown script has defeated every attempt at decryption for over a century, including a 1940s US Army study group led by cryptographer William Friedman, famed for breaking Japanese wartime codes.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Voynich Manuscript (32).jpg

name: Hindenburg
blurb: The largest flying machine ever built caught fire while docking at Lakehurst, New Jersey on 6 May 1937 · radio reporter Herbert Morrison's anguished live broadcast, 'Oh, the humanity!', made it one of the first disasters ever captured in real time.
source: Wikimedia Commons: German airship "Hindenburg" at Lakehurst, New Jersey. - NARA - 518856.tif

name: Washington Monument
blurb: Construction stalled for over two decades and resumed only in 1877 · by then the marble supply had changed, leaving a visible colour change roughly a third of the way up the obelisk that's still there today.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Washington 250424 Washington Monument 01.jpg

name: Al-Aqsa Mosque
blurb: Islam's third-holiest site, first built in the early 8th century AD and rebuilt repeatedly after earthquakes · its silver dome only reached its current look in 1983, replacing an anodized aluminium roof installed after a 1969 arson attack.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Jerusalem-2013-Temple Mount-Al-Aqsa Mosque (NE exposure).jpg

name: Masjid al-Haram
blurb: Rebuilt in 1629 after severe flood damage, the black-draped Kaaba at the heart of Islam's holiest mosque is faced by Muslims worldwide during daily prayers · its Kiswah cloth covering is replaced every year during Hajj, with the old one traditionally cut into pieces for dignitaries.
attribution: Muhammad Sadiq Bey or Ali Bey (attributed)
source: Wikimedia Commons: Kaba (restored).jpg
image_author: Unknown author; on the basis of date, possibly Muhammad Sadiq Bey or Ali Bey, both photographers active in Mecca in 1880

name: Hanging Gardens of Babylon
blurb: Said to have been built by King Nebuchadnezzar II around 600 BC for a homesick wife who missed the mountains of her homeland · no archaeological trace of the gardens has ever been found in Babylon itself, leading some historians to argue they actually stood in Nineveh, over 300 miles away.
source: Wikimedia Commons: Babylon; the city (above); the hanging gardens of Babylon Wellcome L0047679.jpg
